records.reason: CN-01 asks for two things: a batch declares no line figure, and a batch's per-scope total is derived from its member task estimates instead, so no second declaration can drift away from the first. The part concerning BatchDeclaration is the absence, and that absence is guaranteed by the type rather than by behaviour. The declaration holds an identifier and an ordered list of member task ids; its whole declared surface — new(id, task_ids), id(), task_ids(), contains(task_id) — takes no line quantity in, stores none, and returns none. There is therefore no state in which a declared batch total could exist to disagree with the members it summarises, and no run-time observation that could distinguish a compliant declaration from a non-compliant one: a non-compliant one is not constructible. The remaining half of the constraint, the derivation of the per-scope total as the sum of the member estimates, is not this entry's either — BatchDeclaration is handed no estimate at all, and the derivation is declared on the aggregate that holds the estimates. Nothing in this declaration is left over that a test could exercise for CN-01.

IN-14 moves the source of truth for counting a scope's lines out of workflow prose and into the CLI implementation, and fixes that definition: a scope's line figure is additions plus deletions over the committed, staged and unstaged changes measured from the base, untracked files are counted in full as additions, and scope classification reuses the existing review-scope classification mechanism. MeasuredScopeDiff decides none of that. Its declared surface is new(scope, lines), scope() and lines(): it receives a ScopeName and an already-obtained LineCount, stores them, and hands them back unchanged. It reads no worktree, resolves no base, distinguishes no committed from unstaged change, and classifies no file, so not one of the three counting rules is expressible through it. A test bound here could only pass a number to the constructor and read the same number back, which would show the arrangement of the test rather than the counting definition IN-14 promises. That definition is realised by the adapter that produces the figure — a different entry, which does read the worktree and does classify.

AC-17 is checked by observing that the scope line computation exists on the CLI side and that it behaves per the fixed definition: additions plus deletions summed, untracked files counted in full as additions, and the existing review-scope classification mechanism reused. MeasuredScopeDiff is the value that crosses the boundary once such a computation has finished, not the computation. Its declaration — new(scope, lines), scope(), lines() — stores a ScopeName next to a LineCount and returns them unchanged; it holds exactly the same value however the figure was arrived at, so neither the location of the computation nor any of its three counting rules can be observed through it. A test bound to this entry would assert the constructor's storage rather than AC-17's promise. The entry that can exhibit that promise is the one that performs the measurement.

IN-01 promises four things: that batch-plan.json is added as the fourth terminal Phase 3 planning artifact, that impl-planner alone writes it, that the admission-deciding CLI only reads it, and that Phase 3 authoring proceeds in the stated dependency order with each file completed in a single write. BatchPlanDocument is the in-memory model of that artifact's content and reaches none of those facts. It touches no file system, so it cannot observe that the artifact exists or where it sits among the Phase 3 outputs. It holds no notion of an author, a capability contract or a writes-forbidden list, so the single-writer restriction is invisible to it. It carries no history of how the value was produced, so the same document results from any authoring order and from any number of writes; nothing in it distinguishes one authoring sequence from another. The one part that might look testable — that consumers only read — is a property of the declaration rather than of behaviour: the type offers a constructor and borrowing accessors (track_id, task_estimates, batches, estimate_for, batch_of, scope_total, current_batch) and no mutator at all, so a consumer that edits a plan through this type is not expressible and no test can tell a read-only consumer from a writing one. Whatever a test asserted here would restate the type system or the absence of file access rather than IN-01's promise; the evidence the anchor asks for lives in the capability contracts, the workflow's authoring sequence and the CLI wiring, none of which this declaration reaches.

Whatever a test asserted here would restate the type system or the absence of file access rather than AC-01's promise; the evidence the anchor asks for lives in the capability contracts and in the CLI wiring.

ScopeDiffMeasureError is the failure channel of that computation, not the computation: its single MeasureFailed variant carries an opaque diagnostic and appears only when no measurement was produced, so a successful computation — the only kind AC-17 makes a claim about — never reaches this type at all. IN-01 promises that batch-plan.json is added as the fourth terminal Phase 3 planning artifact, that impl-planner alone writes it, that the admission-deciding CLI only reads it, and that Phase 3 authoring proceeds in a fixed dependency order with each file completed in one write. PlanArtifactReadError is the failure channel of a read: two variants, NotFound and ReadFailed with an opaque adapter diagnostic. It has no notion of an author, a capability contract or a writes-forbidden list, so the single-writer restriction is invisible to it; it carries no authoring order, and not even which artifact was being read — the call site knows that, not this value. It is moreover reached only when a read did not produce a document, while every part of IN-01 that could be observed at all concerns an artifact that was successfully authored and read. The read-only nature of this side is a property of the declarations that use it: the ports carrying this error declare a read and no write, so writing through them is not expressible and no test can tell a read-only consumer from a writing one. The evidence IN-01 asks for lives in the capability contracts and the CLI wiring.

AC-01 is checked by two observations: that batch-plan.json exists as a Phase 3 planning artifact, and that its writer is restricted to impl-planner — recorded in the peer capability contracts' writes-forbidden lists, with the admission-deciding CLI reading only. BatchPlanReaderPort is a trait with exactly one method, read, returning a validated document or a read failure. It declares no write operation at all, so 'this consumer only reads' is guaranteed by the type: a writing consumer is not expressible through this port and no run-time observation can distinguish one from the other. The remaining halves — that the artifact exists as a planning output, and that impl-planner is its sole author — are facts about the repository and the capability contracts, neither of which a trait declaration can reach; the port cannot even tell whether the document it received came from that artifact. Any test bound here would restate the method list or the arrangement of its test double rather than AC-01's promise.

IN-14 moves the source of truth for counting a scope's lines into the CLI implementation and fixes that definition: additions plus deletions over the committed, staged and unstaged changes measured from the base, untracked files counted in full as additions, and scope classification reusing the existing review-scope mechanism. ScopeDiffMeasurePort is the seam in front of that work, and its declaration deliberately stops short of it: one method taking an items directory and a track id and returning the resulting figures or a failure. Nothing in that signature counts, sums, classifies or resolves a base — the port cannot express which changes were included or how a file was attributed, because it names none of those things. Any implementation satisfying this declaration is free to count however it likes, so a test bound here can only observe that figures given to a stand-in come back out, which shows the arrangement of the test rather than the counting definition. The definition IN-14 fixes belongs to the adapter behind this seam.

AC-17 is checked by observing that the scope line computation exists on the CLI side and behaves per the fixed definition: additions plus deletions summed, untracked files counted in full as additions, and the existing review-scope classification mechanism reused. ScopeDiffMeasurePort declares only the shape of asking for that computation — an items directory and a track id in, per-scope figures or a failure out. Where the computation lives and how it counts are exactly the things the declaration leaves to whoever implements it, which is why the port can be satisfied by any counting rule at all. No assertion against this trait can therefore establish either half of AC-17's promise; that promise is exhibited by the measuring adapter that reads the worktree and classifies its files.

CN-05 constrains which baseline a measurement is taken from: the per-track commit record, with a fallback to the base branch when that record is missing, corrupt or not an ancestor. ScopeDiffMeasurePort names no baseline. Its single method receives an items directory and a track id and returns the resulting per-scope figures; there is no parameter, return value or error variant through which a baseline choice or a fallback could be observed, and two implementations resolving their baseline completely differently satisfy this declaration identically. The port exposes only the figures precisely so that base resolution stays behind it. A test bound here could assert nothing about CN-05 beyond what its own stand-in was told to return; the constraint is exhibited by the adapter that resolves the base.

IN-07 governs how the declared dependencies of a batch plan constrain batch placement: a task may sit only in a batch at or after the batch of every task it declares a dependency on, and that judgement is made over the task list read from the implementation plan. PlanArtifactReadError is the channel by which such a read reports having produced no task list at all — NotFound when the track declares no such artifact, ReadFailed with an opaque diagnostic when one exists but cannot be decoded. At the moment this value is constructed there is no task, no declared dependency and no batch assignment to compare, so the placement rule has nothing to range over; and when a read does succeed this type never appears, so it cannot colour a placement judgement either. The rule itself is owned by check_batch_plan, whose tests place a declared dependency in a later batch and in the same or an earlier batch and observe the two outcomes. The single property this type does carry — that an absent artifact is reported as a distinct variant instead of being handed on as an empty task list, which would let the placement check pass vacuously — is a property of the type's shape, a variant rather than a fallible default, and so holds by construction. Nothing of IN-07 is left for a test of this type to observe.

AC-07 is checked by observing that the gate returns ERROR for each cross-file structural violation — a task in no batch, a task id naming no existing task, a declared dependency whose target sits in a later batch, and an over-ceiling scope with more than one contributor — and that the batch placement of task pairs declaring no dependency leaves the result unchanged. Every one of those is a judgement over a task list that was read successfully. PlanArtifactReadError is the channel that reports the read never producing such a list: NotFound when the track declares no implementation plan, ReadFailed with an opaque diagnostic otherwise. When it is constructed there is no task list to compare against the batch plan, so not one of AC-07's four violations can be present, let alone asserted; and when the gate does run this type never appears. The distinction it does carry — that an absent plan is reported rather than handed on as an empty task list — is a property of the type's shape, a distinct variant rather than a fallible default, so it holds by construction. Nothing here is left over for a test of AC-07's promise.

AC-05 is accepted by observing that the read side keeps working on what already exists — a schema 1 implementation plan still decodes, the registry and rendered views of a track that is not active still render, and existing track artifacts are not re-verified — and that the gate's subject is the active track, with a missing batch-plan.json on such a track reported as an error. LazyBranchReader takes part in none of that. It discovers the git repository when it is called and returns the name of the branch checked out now, or turns a discovery failure into the port's read error. It opens no track artifact: no implementation plan passes through it, so no schema can be decoded or refused here; no registry or view is rendered from it; and it visits no track directory, so it can neither re-verify a historical artifact nor decline to. The error for an absent batch plan is raised where that artifact is read, by the batch-plan reader and the interactor that maps its NotFound to a failure, and the compatibility of schema 1 is settled inside the implementation-plan codec. What this type supplies is a name, one step before any artifact is opened, and no assertion about artifact compatibility or verification scope can be made of a name. Its own promise is verified where it lives: a discovered repository reports its branch, and an undiscoverable one becomes a read failure at call time rather than at wiring time.

CN-09 is the non-retroactivity rule: the new gate applies only to tracks that are active after its introduction, an absent batch-plan.json on such a track is an error, and the artifacts of earlier tracks stay historical records that are never re-checked. LazyBranchReader can neither honour nor break that rule, because it reads no track artifact whatsoever — it discovers the repository at call time and returns the current branch name, or the port's read error when discovery fails. Which tracks are checked is decided by the readers that open a track directory and by the interactor that drives them; whether an earlier track's artifacts are revisited is decided the same way, by nobody visiting them. The error for a missing batch plan belongs to the batch-plan reader path. Even the fact that a branch name refers to the checkout of the moment is a property of what git reports rather than a decision this type makes, so there is nothing here to assert about retroactivity. Its own promise — a discovered repository reports its branch, an undiscoverable one fails at call time rather than at wiring time — is verified where it lives.
